definition: A statement of what a user or stakeholder needs the product to achieve, written in that person's terms.
wrongs: A choice of database brand made by a programmer.
The colour of an internal log file.
A line of code that implements a loop.
why: A user requirement states a need in stakeholder language, before technical design decisions are made.
example: Students need to see today's classes on a phone without asking the faculty office.
scenario: Students say they need today's classes on a phone without visiting the office. Which kind of statement is that?
scenarioWrongs: The colour of a log file
scenarioWhy: A need expressed in the user's terms is a user requirement.

definition: A statement of what the product as a whole must do or constrain, derived from user needs and technical limits.
wrongs: A personal preference of one developer that no stakeholder asked for.
The project team's favourite meeting time.
A slogan on the poster for the demonstration.
why: A system requirement states a product-level behaviour or constraint derived from needs and real limits.
example: The product must show a student's timetable from the faculty feed and work when the phone is offline for cached days.
scenario: The product must show the faculty timetable feed and keep cached days available offline. Which statement is that?
scenarioWhy: A product-level obligation derived from the user need is a system requirement.

definition: A required behaviour of the product, such as an action it must perform for a user.
wrongs: A target for response time or availability that names no behaviour.
The budget of the student project.
The font used on the title slide.
why: A functional requirement names behaviour the product must provide, not a quality level or a budget.
example: The app must let a student filter today's classes by module code.
scenario: The app must let a student filter today's classes by module code. Which kind of requirement is that?
scenarioWrongs: A two-second response target with no behaviour
scenarioWhy: Filtering classes is a behaviour the product must perform, so the statement is functional.

definition: A required quality of the product, such as performance, reliability, security, or usability.
wrongs: A named function, such as creating an account.
The name of the team leader.
A list of who will bring snacks to the demo.
why: A non-functional requirement states how well the product must work, not which function it offers.
example: The timetable screen must appear within two seconds on the agreed campus network.
scenario: The timetable screen must appear within two seconds on the campus network. Which kind of requirement is that?
scenarioWrongs: A function that creates an account
scenarioWhy: A response-time quality is a non-functional requirement.

definition: The ability to follow a requirement from its source through design and tests to the feature that satisfies it.
wrongs: Remembering requirements only in conversation, with no link to tests.
Numbering paragraphs in a novel.
Tracing a parcel through a courier company.
why: Traceability links each requirement to the design and tests that show it has been met.
example: Requirement R4 is linked to the filter screen in the design and to test case T12.
scenario: A marker asks which test shows that the module-code filter was implemented. Which capability answers that?
scenarioWhy: Traceability follows a requirement through design to the test that demonstrates it.

definition: A table that links each requirement to the design elements and test cases that cover it.
wrongs: A Gantt chart of task dates.
A table of team members' phone numbers.
A matrix of risk scores with no requirements.
why: A traceability matrix is the table that makes coverage of requirements by design and tests visible.
example: The matrix row for R4 lists the filter screen and test cases T12 and T13.
scenario: You need one table showing each requirement, its design element, and its tests. Which artefact is that?
scenarioWhy: A traceability matrix is the table linking requirements to design elements and test cases.

definition: A description of how an actor achieves a goal with the system, including the main steps and important alternatives.
wrongs: A class diagram that shows only software structure.
A one-line wish with no steps.
A test log of defects already found.
why: A use case describes an actor's goal, the main flow, and notable alternatives.
example: The use case View today shows a student opening the app, seeing classes, and the alternative when the feed is down.
scenario: You must describe the student's steps to see today's classes, including the feed-down alternative. Which description is that?
scenarioWrongs: A class diagram of code structure
A one-line wish with no steps
scenarioWhy: A use case records the actor's goal, main steps, and important alternatives.

definition: A short requirement in the form of who wants what and why, used to plan a slice of user-visible value.
wrongs: A detailed database schema.
A full test script with inputs and expected rows.
A story written for entertainment with no user or goal.
why: A user story captures who wants a capability and why, at a size the team can plan.
example: As a student, I want to filter by module code so I can find one class quickly.
scenario: The team writes: as a student I want to filter by module so I can find a class quickly. Which artefact is that?
scenarioWrongs: A fictional story with no user need
scenarioWhy: A short who-wants-what-and-why statement used for planning is a user story.

definition: The conditions a requirement or story must meet before the team and sponsor agree it is done.
wrongs: The date the coding happened to stop.
A developer's feeling that the screen looks finished.
The number of commits in the repository.
why: Acceptance criteria are the agreed conditions that define done for a requirement or story.
example: The filter is done only when a known module code shows that module's classes and an unknown code shows a clear message.
scenario: The sponsor will accept the filter only if a known code lists the right classes and an unknown code shows a message. Which term names those conditions?
scenarioWrongs: A feeling that the screen looks done
scenarioWhy: Acceptance criteria are the agreed conditions that must be met before the story is accepted.

definition: A named set of responsibilities given to a member so the group covers requirements, build, test, and coordination.
wrongs: A person's hobby outside the project.
A job title at a company the student does not work for.
A role that nobody can describe and that has no responsibilities.
why: A team role assigns clear responsibilities so necessary project work has an owner.
example: One member owns requirements, another owns integration, and another owns the test records.
scenario: Work is being missed because nobody owns the test records. Which fix uses team roles?
scenarioAnswer: Name a member responsible for the test records
scenarioWrongs: Copy a job title from an unrelated company
scenarioWhy: A team role gives a named member the responsibilities that were otherwise missing.

definition: The member who coordinates the group, tracks commitments, and keeps decisions and blockers visible.
wrongs: The person who writes every line of code alone while others wait.
A sponsor outside the team who never coordinates the members.
The repository, which cannot coordinate people.
why: The team leader coordinates people and commitments; they are not required to produce every technical artefact alone.
example: The leader keeps the task board current and raises a blocker when the faculty feed is unavailable.
scenario: Commitments are slipping and blockers are invisible. Which role should make them visible and coordinate the group?
scenarioWrongs: A member who writes all the code alone
An external sponsor who does not coordinate the team
scenarioWhy: The team leader coordinates the group and keeps commitments and blockers visible.

definition: The member accountable for eliciting, recording, and keeping requirements consistent and agreed.
wrongs: The member whose only job is to run performance tests.
A user who mentions a wish once and never reviews the record.
The person who only designs the poster.
why: The requirements lead owns the quality and agreement of the requirement set.
example: The requirements lead updates the filter story after the sponsor clarifies unknown module codes.
scenario: Stories contradict each other and nobody has checked them with the sponsor. Which role should fix that?
scenarioWrongs: The person who only runs performance tests
A user who never reviews the record
scenarioWhy: The requirements lead keeps requirements consistent and agreed with stakeholders.

definition: The member accountable for planning how components come together and for resolving interface mismatches.
wrongs: The member who only writes the user manual.
A tester who never sees the interfaces.
The sponsor who only attends the final demo.
why: The integration lead plans the combination of components and deals with mismatches at their boundaries.
example: When the app and the faculty feed disagree on date format, the integration lead gets the interface corrected.
scenario: The app and the faculty feed disagree on date format at their boundary. Which role should drive the fix?
scenarioWrongs: A tester who never sees interfaces
A sponsor who only attends the final demo
scenarioWhy: Resolving an interface mismatch is the integration lead's responsibility.

definition: The member accountable for the test approach, the test cases, and the record of results against requirements.
wrongs: A developer who refuses to record any test result.
The graphic designer of the logo.
A teammate who only books meeting rooms.
why: The test lead owns how the product will be tested and how results are traced to requirements.
example: The test lead maps each story to test cases and publishes which ones passed before the demonstration.
scenario: The demo is soon and nobody knows which requirements have passed their tests. Which role should produce that record?
scenarioWrongs: A developer who keeps no results
The person who only books rooms
scenarioWhy: The test lead is accountable for test cases and the record of results against requirements.

definition: A versioned product of the project, such as a document, source module, or build, that is identified and controlled.
wrongs: An unlabelled file that anyone may overwrite with no history.
A team member's mood.
The weather on demo day.
why: A configuration item is an identified, versioned artefact the project controls.
example: The interface specification is stored as version 1.3, and later edits create a new version rather than a silent overwrite.
scenario: The interface specification must be identifiable and changes must not overwrite it silently. How should it be treated?
scenarioWrongs: As an unlabelled file anyone may overwrite
scenarioWhy: A controlled, versioned project artefact is a configuration item.

definition: A description of how two components exchange data or calls, including formats, order, and error cases.
wrongs: A photo of the two teams that built the components.
A user's wish with no data format.
The office seating plan.
why: An interface specification defines the shared boundary so components can be built and tested against the same contract.
example: The spec says the feed sends module code as text, date as ISO-8601, and error code 404 when the student is unknown.
scenario: The app team and the feed team need an agreed date format and error codes. Which document should hold that agreement?
scenarioWhy: An interface specification defines formats, sequences, and error cases between components.

definition: The work of combining components so they operate together as one product, not only as separate parts.
wrongs: Testing a single function with no other component attached.
Writing the project poster.
Merging two social groups at a party.
why: System integration combines components and checks that they work together as a product.
example: The timetable screen is connected to the live faculty feed and shows real classes rather than hardcoded samples.
scenario: The screen works with fake data, but it has never been connected to the live faculty feed. Which work is still missing?
scenarioWhy: Connecting components so they work as one product is system integration.

definition: The planned order and method for combining components, chosen so interface defects can be found.
wrongs: Combining parts in whatever order people finish, with no plan.
A marketing plan for the demonstration.
The algorithm inside one function.
why: An integration strategy decides the order and method of combination so interface problems are found deliberately.
example: The team plans to connect the feed first, then notifications, testing each join before adding the next part.
scenario: Components will finish at different times, and the team needs a deliberate order for joining them. Which plan is that?
scenarioWrongs: Joining parts in whatever order they finish
scenarioWhy: The planned order and method for combining components is the integration strategy.

definition: An approach that combines all components in one step, which delays discovery of interface defects until late.
wrongs: Adding one component at a time and testing after each addition.
Testing a single module before any joining.
A demonstration that shows only slides.
why: Big-bang integration waits until every component is present, so interface faults appear late and are harder to isolate.
example: The team connects feed, login, and notifications on the final weekend and cannot tell which join caused the date errors.
scenario: All unfinished parts will be connected on the last weekend, with no earlier joins. Which approach is that?
scenarioWrongs: Adding and testing one component at a time
A unit test of a single module
scenarioWhy: Combining every component in one late step is big-bang integration.

definition: An approach that adds components in planned stages and tests each stage before the next component is added.
wrongs: Waiting to combine every component in a single final step.
Never combining components at all.
Adding features to a slide deck one bullet at a time.
why: Incremental integration tests each added component so a new interface fault can be tied to the latest change.
example: The feed is integrated and tested before notifications are added, so a later fault is easier to locate.
scenario: The team adds the feed, tests it, then adds notifications. Which integration approach is that?
scenarioWrongs: Connecting everything in one final step
scenarioWhy: Adding components in stages and testing each stage is incremental integration.

definition: A test of a single module or function in isolation from the rest of the product.
wrongs: A test of several components talking across their interfaces.
A test of the whole product in a realistic environment.
A sponsor's check against the original business need.
why: A unit test isolates one module so a failure points to that module rather than to an interface.
example: A test calls the date parser with an ISO string and does not start the faculty feed or the phone app.
scenario: You want to check the date parser alone, without the feed or the app. Which test fits?
scenarioWrongs: A test of several components together
A test of the finished product on campus
scenarioWhy: Testing one module in isolation is a unit test.

definition: A test that checks whether combined components communicate and behave correctly across their interfaces.
wrongs: A test of one function with all neighbours replaced and no real interface.
A spelling check of the user manual.
A review of the project budget.
why: Integration tests target the joins between components, which unit tests deliberately avoid.
example: A test requests today's classes through the app's client and checks the parsed response from the faculty feed.
scenario: The date parser works alone, but you must check that the app and the feed exchange dates correctly. Which test fits?
scenarioWrongs: A spelling check of the manual
scenarioWhy: Checking behaviour across the join between components is an integration test.

definition: A test of the completed product against system requirements, in an environment close to intended use.
wrongs: A test of one function on a developer's machine with stubs only.
A code review that does not execute the product.
A test of a single interface with the rest missing.
why: System testing executes the whole product against system requirements in a realistic setting.
example: On a campus phone and network, testers check that the full app meets the timetable requirements end to end.
scenario: The full app must be checked against timetable requirements on a campus phone and network. Which test level is that?
scenarioWrongs: A code review that does not run the product
A test of one interface with the rest absent
scenarioWhy: Testing the completed product against system requirements in a near-real environment is system testing.

definition: A test, often with the sponsor or users, that checks the product against the agreed acceptance criteria.
wrongs: A developer's private check that never involves the agreed criteria.
A unit test of a helper function.
A rehearsal of who will speak, with the product switched off.
why: Acceptance testing judges the product against the criteria the sponsor or users agreed.
example: The faculty officer tries the filter with a real module code and confirms the acceptance message for an unknown code.
scenario: The faculty officer will judge the filter against the agreed done conditions. Which test is that?
scenarioWrongs: A private check with no agreed criteria
A unit test of a helper
A speaking rehearsal with the product off
scenarioWhy: A check against agreed acceptance criteria, often by the sponsor or user, is an acceptance test.

definition: A specified set of preconditions, inputs, steps, and expected results used to check one aspect of the product.
wrongs: A vague note that says try the app.
The requirement text with no inputs or expected result.
A list of team members.
why: A test case specifies how to perform a check and what result counts as a pass.
example: Test T12 sets a known module code, opens today's view, and expects only that module's classes.
scenario: You must specify the input, steps, and expected classes for the module filter. Which artefact is that?
scenarioWrongs: A note that only says try the app
The requirement with no expected result
scenarioWhy: A test case states preconditions, inputs, steps, and the expected result.

definition: The outcome a test should produce if the requirement has been implemented correctly.
wrongs: Whatever the current buggy build happens to show.
The tester's guess written after seeing the failure.
The time the test happened to finish.
why: The expected result is defined from the requirement so the actual outcome can be judged as pass or fail.
example: For an unknown module code, the expected result is the message No classes for that code and an empty list.
scenario: An unknown module code is entered. Which outcome should be written as the expected result before the test is run?
scenarioAnswer: The agreed message and an empty class list
scenarioWrongs: A guess written after seeing the failure
The clock time when the test ended
scenarioWhy: The expected result is the correct outcome defined before execution, used to judge pass or fail.

definition: A flaw in the product or its documentation that causes it to miss a requirement or an agreed standard.
wrongs: A change request for behaviour nobody had agreed.
A passing test.
A team member's absence.
why: A defect is a failure to meet an agreed requirement or standard, not a new wish or a staffing issue.
example: The app shows classes for the wrong day, which breaks the requirement to show today's timetable.
scenario: The app shows the wrong day's classes, contrary to the agreed requirement. Which item should be logged?
scenarioWrongs: A new wish that was never agreed
scenarioWhy: Behaviour that misses an agreed requirement is a defect.

definition: A rating of how serious a defect's effect is on users or on meeting requirements, separate from how soon it will be fixed.
wrongs: The order in which the team chooses to fix defects, which is priority.
The number of lines changed in the fix.
The tester's seniority.
why: Severity rates the effect of the defect; priority is a separate decision about fix order.
example: A crash on login is rated high severity even though the team schedules the fix after a smaller text change.
scenario: Login crashes for every user, but the team will fix a typo first for the demo. Which rating describes the crash's effect?
scenarioWrongs: Low severity because the typo is fixed first
Severity equal to the number of lines in the fix
Severity equal to the tester's year of study
scenarioWhy: Severity rates the crash's effect on users, independently of the order chosen for fixes.

definition: A test run after a change to check that behaviour which previously worked still works.
wrongs: The first test of a brand-new feature that never worked before.
A test skipped because the change looked small.
A review of the project risks.
why: Regression testing protects existing behaviour from being broken by a later change.
example: After the date-format fix, the team reruns the previously passing login tests.
scenario: A date-format fix might have broken login, which used to pass. Which tests should be rerun?
scenarioAnswer: Regression tests of the previously passing login behaviour
scenarioWrongs: Only a test of a feature that never existed
No tests, because the change looked small
A review of the risk register
scenarioWhy: Regression tests check that behaviour which already worked still works after a change.

definition: A planned examination of a design against requirements, held so defects can be raised before build continues.
wrongs: A demonstration of the finished product after build is complete.
An unplanned chat with no design and no record.
A test that executes code.
why: A design review checks the design against requirements early enough for defects to be fixed before further build.
example: Peers review the timetable screen design and note that offline cached days are missing from the agreed requirements.
scenario: The screen design is ready, but coding of it has not started. You want peers to find gaps against requirements. Which event fits?
scenarioWrongs: The final demonstration after everything is built
An unrecorded chat with no design present
Executing the code in a test
scenarioWhy: A design review examines the design against requirements before build continues.

definition: An examination of a work product by colleagues who did not create it, aimed at finding defects early.
wrongs: The author reading their own work and declaring it correct.
A manager approving a budget.
A user test of the finished app.
why: Peer review uses colleagues other than the author to find defects in a work product.
example: Two teammates who did not write the interface spec check it for missing error codes.
scenario: The author of the interface spec wants others to hunt for missing error cases. Which activity fits?
scenarioAnswer: A peer review by people who did not write the spec
scenarioWrongs: The author approving their own spec alone
A user test of the finished app
scenarioWhy: Peer review is an examination by colleagues who did not create the work product.

definition: A review in which the author leads others through a work product step by step to collect comments.
wrongs: A review where the author is absent and reviewers work only from the document.
A fire drill in the building.
A silent approval with no walk through the content.
why: In a walkthrough the author guides the group through the work so questions and comments can be gathered.
example: The author presents each screen of the timetable flow, and reviewers comment on the offline step.
scenario: The author will lead the group through each screen of the flow to collect comments. Which review form is that?
scenarioWrongs: A review held with the author absent
A silent approval with no examination
scenarioWhy: A walkthrough is author-led, step-by-step presentation of a work product to gather comments.

definition: Written material that describes the design, interfaces, and operation so others can build, test, or maintain the product.
wrongs: A poster whose only purpose is to attract an audience to the demo.
An empty repository with no explanation.
A chat reaction emoji.
why: Technical documentation explains the product well enough for someone else to build, test, or maintain it.
example: The repository includes the architecture notes, the feed interface, and the steps to run the app locally.
scenario: A marker who did not build the app must be able to understand the design and run it. Which material is required?
scenarioAnswer: Technical documentation of design, interfaces, and run steps
scenarioWrongs: An emoji in the team chat
scenarioWhy: Technical documentation describes design, interfaces, and operation for people who must build, test, or maintain the product.

definition: A document that records design decisions and structure in enough detail for the team to implement them consistently.
wrongs: A user manual written only for end users after delivery.
A list of wishes with no design decisions.
The test results from the last run.
why: A design specification captures decisions and structure so implementers follow the same design.
example: The specification shows the screen structure, the cached-day rule, and how module filtering is applied.
scenario: Two developers must implement filtering the same way. Which document should record that design decision?
scenarioWrongs: A wish list with no decisions
scenarioWhy: The design specification records structural decisions so implementation stays consistent.

definition: A document that explains how an end user performs tasks with the finished product.
wrongs: A design specification aimed at implementers.
The source code itself.
A risk register.
why: A user manual is written for end users and explains tasks, not internal design.
example: The manual tells a student how to open today's view and filter by module code.
scenario: Students need instructions for filtering classes, without internal design detail. Which document fits?
scenarioWhy: A user manual explains end-user tasks with the finished product.

definition: A description of a programming interface, including operations, inputs, return values, and error conditions.
wrongs: A guide showing only button clicks for a non-programmer.
A photograph of the server.
The team's meeting minutes.
why: API documentation tells a programmer how to call an interface and what it returns, including errors.
example: The feed docs list the timetable operation, the student-id parameter, the class list returned, and the unknown-student error.
scenario: Another team must call your timetable operation correctly, including errors. Which document should you give them?
scenarioWhy: API documentation describes operations, inputs, return values, and error conditions.

definition: A drawing that shows the major components of the product and how they connect.
wrongs: A sketch of the classroom furniture.
A sequence of every source-code line.
A pie chart of the marks scheme.
why: An architecture diagram communicates structure: the main parts and their connections.
example: The diagram shows the phone app, the campus API, and the faculty feed, with arrows for timetable requests.
scenario: The marker wants to see the app, the API, and the faculty feed and how they connect. Which drawing fits?
scenarioWrongs: A sketch of the classroom furniture
A listing of every code line
scenarioWhy: An architecture diagram shows major components and the connections among them.

definition: A system that records changes to project files over time so the team can compare, recover, and merge work.
wrongs: Emailing files named final, final2, and final-really.
A paper notebook of meeting dates.
The undo button in a drawing tool used by one person with no shared history.
why: Version control keeps a shared history of changes so work can be recovered and combined.
example: Two members edit the app on branches, then merge, and can still recover yesterday's working version.
scenario: Two members are editing the same app and must merge without losing yesterday's working version. Which system supports that?
scenarioWrongs: Emailing copies named final and final2
One person's undo button with no shared history
scenarioWhy: Version control records file history so the team can merge work and recover earlier versions.

definition: An agreed version of a requirement, design, or build that later changes must pass through change control.
wrongs: A draft that anyone may change silently.
The first rough idea, never reviewed.
A personal backup on one laptop that the team has not agreed.
why: A baseline is an agreed reference; changing it requires the project's change-control steps.
example: After the sponsor agrees the stories, that set is baselined and further story changes are requested formally.
scenario: The sponsor has agreed the stories, and later edits must be approved rather than made silently. Which status should that set have?
scenarioWhy: An agreed version that cannot change without control is a baseline.

definition: The process for proposing, assessing, approving, and recording changes to baselined requirements or design.
wrongs: Editing the baselined story in the repository with no record.
Refusing every change even when the sponsor requests one.
A version-control commit message alone, with no assessment or approval.
why: Change control makes a baseline change visible, assessed, and approved before it is adopted.
example: Adding offline mode after baseline is written up, estimated, approved by the sponsor, and then added to the stories.
scenario: After baseline, the sponsor wants offline mode. Which process should the team follow before building it?
scenarioWrongs: A silent edit to the baselined stories
An automatic refusal of every sponsor request
A commit with no assessment or approval
scenarioWhy: Change control proposes, assesses, approves, and records a change to a baseline.

definition: A live showing of the working product to stakeholders so they can see that agreed behaviour is present.
wrongs: A slide talk with the product switched off.
A private test nobody else sees.
A poster session with no running software.
why: A demonstration uses the working product so stakeholders can observe agreed behaviour.
example: At the review the team opens the app, filters a real module, and shows the unknown-code message.
scenario: The sponsor wants to see the filter work, not only hear about it. Which event meets that request?
scenarioAnswer: A live demonstration of the working app
scenarioWrongs: Slides with the product switched off
A private test with no sponsor
A poster and no running software
scenarioWhy: A demonstration shows the working product performing the agreed behaviour.

definition: A planned sequence of steps and talking points so a demonstration covers the agreed scenarios.
wrongs: An improvised click-through with no check that agreed scenarios appear.
The full source code read aloud.
A script for a film unrelated to the product.
why: A demo script keeps the live showing focused on the scenarios the team agreed to present.
example: The script says: log in as a student, open today, filter module CS101, then enter an unknown code.
scenario: The team must be sure the demo covers login, today's view, a known module, and an unknown code. Which aid should they follow?
scenarioWrongs: A film script about another topic
scenarioWhy: A demo script is the planned sequence that covers the agreed scenarios.

definition: An early partial version of the product, built to explore or check a design with users or the team.
wrongs: The finished product accepted for delivery.
A written requirement with nothing a user can try.
A poster of the team logo.
why: A prototype is a partial build used to learn about the design, not the accepted final product.
example: The team shows a clickable timetable screen with fake data so students can comment before the feed is connected.
scenario: Students should try the screen layout before the live feed exists. Which build fits that purpose?
scenarioAnswer: A prototype with the layout and fake data
scenarioWrongs: A requirement paragraph with nothing to try
scenarioWhy: A prototype is an early partial version used to check a design with users.

definition: A small build used to test whether a risky technical idea works, not to deliver the full product.
wrongs: The complete app with every story finished.
A literature essay about the idea.
A user manual for features that already exist.
why: A proof of concept answers a narrow technical question and is not the delivered product.
example: The team builds a tiny client that only checks whether the faculty feed accepts the campus login token.
scenario: Nobody knows whether the faculty feed will accept the campus login token. Which build should answer that before full development?
scenarioAnswer: A proof of concept that only tests the token
scenarioWrongs: The finished app with every story
A manual for features already delivered
scenarioWhy: A proof of concept is a small build that tests one risky technical idea.

definition: A scheduled demonstration tied to a project milestone, used to show progress and collect stakeholder feedback.
wrongs: An unscheduled desk check with no milestone and no stakeholders.
The final exam of an unrelated module.
A demonstration held after the module has already closed and no feedback can be used.
why: A milestone demonstration is planned against a milestone so progress is visible and feedback can still be used.
example: At the mid-project milestone the team demonstrates login and today's view and records the sponsor's comments.
scenario: The mid-project milestone requires stakeholders to see login and today's view and to give comments you can still use. Which event is that?
scenarioWrongs: A private desk check with no milestone
A showing after the module has closed
scenarioWhy: A milestone demonstration is a scheduled showing at a milestone that gathers usable feedback.

definition: The management of agreements about interfaces so a shared boundary is not changed without informing the other parties.
wrongs: Each team changing the shared date format whenever it likes.
A ban on ever writing an interface specification.
Controlling only the office door keys.
why: Interface control keeps agreed boundaries stable unless a change is communicated and agreed.
example: The feed team cannot switch the date format until the app team has agreed an update to the interface specification.
scenario: The feed team wants to change the date format the app already uses. Which practice stops a silent break?
scenarioAnswer: Interface control that requires agreement before the change
scenarioWrongs: Changing the format whenever the feed team likes
Having no written interface at all
scenarioWhy: Interface control stops a shared boundary changing unless the other parties are informed and agree.

definition: A stand-in for a component that is not ready, returning canned responses so its caller can be tested.
wrongs: The finished faculty feed in production.
A program that calls the component under test and supplies inputs.
A user manual.
why: A stub replaces a missing dependency and returns predetermined responses to the component being tested.
example: Until the faculty feed exists, a stub returns two fixed classes when the app requests today.
scenario: The app must be tested before the faculty feed exists. Which stand-in returns fixed classes to the app?
scenarioWrongs: A driver that calls the app
scenarioWhy: A stub stands in for a missing component and returns canned responses to its caller.

definition: A temporary program that calls a component under test and supplies inputs when the real caller is not ready.
wrongs: A stand-in that replaces a component the code under test needs to call.
The production mobile app shipped to students.
A person who drives the team to the demo.
why: A driver calls the component being tested; a stub is what the component calls when a dependency is missing.
example: A small program calls the date parser with sample strings because the app screens are not ready.
scenario: The date parser is ready, but the app that should call it is not. Which temporary program can supply inputs and call the parser?
scenarioWrongs: A stub that replaces the parser
A car journey to the demo
scenarioWhy: A test driver is a temporary caller that supplies inputs to a component whose real caller is not ready.

definition: An assembled version of the product, identified so testers know exactly which revision they ran.
wrongs: A pile of uncompiled source with no identifiable output.
The requirements document.
A verbal claim that it works on someone's machine.
why: A build is a specific assembled revision that can be named, tested, and reproduced.
example: Testers install build 0.4, identified by its commit, and record results against that identifier.
scenario: Testers must record exactly which assembled app they ran. Which identifier should they cite?
scenarioWrongs: An unnamed pile of source files
A verbal claim with no revision
scenarioWhy: A build is an identified assembled version so test results refer to a known revision.

definition: A short document that lists what a build contains, which defects were fixed, and any known limits.
wrongs: The full design specification.
A blank file attached to the build.
A marketing slogan with no build contents.
why: Release notes tell users and testers what changed in a build and what is still limited.
example: The note for build 0.4 says module filtering was added, the wrong-day defect was fixed, and offline mode is still absent.
scenario: Testers receive build 0.4 and need to know what changed and what is still missing. Which document should accompany it?
scenarioWhy: A release note lists the build's contents, fixes, and known limits.
